content: If there is a risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV, the correct and consistent use of condoms is strongly recommended. When used properly and consistently, condoms provide one of the most effective methods of protection against STIs, including HIV. Female condoms are also effective and safe; however, they are not as widely utilized in national programs compared to male condoms. Women with medical conditions that make pregnancy an unacceptable risk should be informed that barrier methods for pregnancy prevention may not be suitable for those who cannot use them consistently and correctly due to their relatively higher failure rates with typical use. For individuals with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4), the use of spermicides and diaphragms (with spermicide) can disrupt the cervical mucosa, potentially increasing viral shedding and the risk of HIV transmission to uninfected sexual partners. Similarly, in cases of asymptomatic or mild HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 1 or 2), the use of these methods may also lead to increased viral shedding and transmission risk. Toxic shock syndrome has been reported in association with diaphragm use. Additionally, repeated and high-dose use of nonoxynol-9 spermicide can cause vaginal and cervical irritation or abrasions, which may increase susceptibility to infections, including HIV. For women who are breastfeeding, fertility awareness-based (FAB) methods may be less effective than when not breastfeeding. During the first six weeks postpartum, women who are exclusively breastfeeding and amenorrheic are unlikely to exhibit detectable fertility signs or hormonal changes. However, the likelihood of resuming fertility increases with time postpartum and with the introduction of supplemental feeding. Non-breastfeeding women are unlikely to require FAB methods or exhibit detectable fertility signs or hormonal changes within the first four weeks postpartum. After four weeks, ovarian function typically resumes, and FAB methods may become applicable. Women can use calendar-based methods after completing at least three postpartum menstrual cycles with regularity. The Standard Days Method can be used after at least four postpartum menstrual cycles if the most recent cycle was 26–32 days long. Post-abortion, women are likely to regain sufficient ovarian function to exhibit detectable fertility signs and hormonal changes. Calendar-based methods can be initiated after at least one post-abortion menstrual cycle. If prior cycles were 26–32 days long, the Standard Days Method may also be used. Until then, alternative contraceptive methods appropriate for the post-abortion period should be offered. The lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) does not protect against STIs, including HIV. If there is a risk of STI/HIV, the correct and consistent use of condoms is recommended.
